Improved quality and reproducibility of cerebral cortical organoids under microfluidic culture conditions: a proof-of-concept study
papers.abstract: Cerebral organoids have emerged as advanced three-dimensional in vitro models capable of recapitulating essential aspects of human brain development, thereby offering new opportunities for studying brain physiology and disease. Nonetheless, their use in preclinical settings remains limited by their high variability. Microfluidic devices offer a promising alternative to conventional culture supports by enabling improved recapitulation of the cellular microenvironment; however, most cerebral organoids-on-chips rely on custom-made academic prototypes, limiting their scalability and translatability. Here, we established a standardized brain organoid-on-chip model by combining a regionalized cortical organoid differentiation protocol with a commercially available microfluidic device (Duplex™, NETRI). Cortical organoid quality and reproducibility were evaluated using a previously established multi-criteria Quality Control (QC) framework based on a scoring system. To enhance objectivity and throughput, the non-invasive morphometric QC criteria were automated using deep learning-based image analysis. Using a single human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) line, we assessed whether microfluidic culture conditions could improve the quality and reproducibility of cortical organoids within a controlled genetic background. Compared with conventional cultures, on-chip cortical organoids displayed improved inter- and intra-batch reproducibility across multiple scales, including morphology, size, cytoarchitectural organization, and transcript expression, together with higher QC scores and reduced QC failure rates. Finally, the QC framework was adapted for neurotoxicity assessment using a decision tree to classify compounds according to their neurotoxic risk. While this study represents a proof-of-concept demonstration within a single genetic background, the integrated brain organoid-on-chip platform and standardized QC evaluations provide a flexible and translatable approach for preclinical and industrial studies and support future validation across multiple hiPSC lines.

papers.title: Enhancing the structural integrity of 3D bioprinted urethral grafts for clinical applications using GelMA–fibrinogen bioinks infused with human primary cells
papers.abstract: The demand for organ transplantation continues to grow, while challenges remain, such as the shortage of organ donors and complications associated with existing treatments. A promising alternative to transplantation is the implantation of artificial organs, which can be produced using 3D bioprinting technology. This approach offers the advantage of patient-specific solutions tailored to individual needs. Patients with urethral stricture or hypospadias who are unable to urinate require urethral reconstruction, which carries risks of complications and restricture. These patients may benefit from a tissue-engineered urethra fabricated using autologous cells and 3D bioprinting.A printer setup for tubular structures was developed for a 3D-Bioplotter and a gelatin-fibrinogen-based bioink was supplemented with GelMA to enhance mechanical properties for clinical applications while maintaining cell compatibility. Evaluation was performed through tensile testing, printability, suturability and cell viability analyses. An artificial urethral graft was successfully fabricated, demonstrating the operational capacity of our rod-based printer setup and the GelMA-fibrinogen hydrogel exhibited an increase in Young’s modulus compared with the gelatin-fibrinogen hydrogel. The GelMA-fibrinogen hydrogel also exhibited good suturability and efficient cell recovery after 14 days of culture. Human urothelial- and smooth muscle cells developed characteristic morphologies within the print, and a 210% increase in burst pressure was observed for the urethral graft after 14 days of culture, compared with the acellular graft.This 3D bioprinted artificial urethra, containing human urothelial and smooth muscle cells, represents a significant step forward in developing new treatment options for urethral disorders.

Robotic winding of wet-spun fibers for biofabrication of aligned, perfusable, muscle-based tissue
papers.abstract: Structural alignment of muscle and integrated vasculature enables the function of geometrically complex tissues in the body, such as the gastroesophageal junction and the ventricles. However, replicating this complexity is an ongoing challenge. Described here is the wet-spun & robotically articulated placement (WRAP) method for deposition of aligned cellular fibers on scaffolds, resulting in large structures fabricated from the inside-out. WRAP enables complex, multi-oriented muscle and vascular placement by creating a continuous cellular fiber through wet spinning, and then using a robotic arm programmed with a set of tissue profiles to maneuver the fiber around an organ scaffold. Wet-spun fibers, consisting of muscle cells combined with endothelial cell fibers via double-core spinning, exhibited the ability to mature, align, contract, and initiate tubulogenesis, creating perfusable fibers. Further, the robotic arm could accurately create physiologically relevant fiber patterns with high precision. The potential to generate perfusable blood vessels alongside functional muscle is paramount to fabricating muscle-based constructs. The WRAP method offers a high throughput and versatile solution to the scale-up problem plaguing the biofabrication of muscle-based tissues.

Mesenchymal stem cell-derived spheroids and microtissues for biofabrication: advances in bioassembly and bioprinting strategies
papers.abstract: Biofabrication integrates biological and engineering principles to generate functional tissues for regenerative medicine, drug screening, and disease modeling. Among the diverse cellular sources available, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have emerged as a critical component due to their multipotency, immunomodulatory capacity, and scalability. This review focuses on MSC-derived spheroids and microtissues as building blocks for biofabrication, organizing recent advances in bioassembly and bioprinting strategies around the axis of undifferentiated versus pre-differentiated microtissues and how the timing of differentiation shapes construct functionality. Key technological innovations, including dynamic culture systems, scaffold-free assembly, and high-resolution bioprinting (e.g. droplet-based), have enabled enhanced control over microtissue maturation and structural fidelity. The role of the cellular microenvironment in determining MSC fate is examined, emphasizing how biochemical cues, mechanical properties, and oxygen gradients can be engineered during microtissue formation. Cellular heterogeneity is addressed as a path-dependent variable continuously reshaped by donor-specific factors (age, sex, health status) and process-imposed cues (isolation methods, expansion conditions, and mechanical stress) throughout the in vitro life cycle, and concrete mitigation strategies are discussed, including prospective cell sorting and a proposed functional potency panel (extracellular matrix deposition, fusion competence, and secretome profiling), alongside recent advancements in automated and machine learning-based biofabrication platforms. Vascularization and immunological integration are examined as central translation bottlenecks, covering endothelial co-culture, prevascularized spheroids, sacrificial bioprinting, and MSC-driven modulation of the host immune response. By integrating the fabrication route, heterogeneity as a manufacturing process variable, and translational/regulatory bottlenecks into a single framework, this review highlights recent advances, discusses current limitations, and outlines future directions for clinical translation of MSC-based biofabrication.

MLATE V3: an open-source multi-tissue AI framework for data-driven optimization of 3D printed and bioprinted scaffolds
papers.abstract: 3D (bio)printing is increasingly used for scaffold fabrication in tissue engineering; however, identifying suitable biomaterial compositions, cell types, cell densities, and printing conditions remains largely empirical, time-consuming, and costly. Practical application of machine learning (ML) in this field is further limited by the scarcity of comprehensive datasets based on pre-fabrication variables, the lack of integrated frameworks for prioritizing candidate scaffold formulations, and the limited availability of accessible tools for non-technical users. To address these challenges, we developed MLATE V3 (Machine Learning Applications in Tissue Engineering V3), an open-source, data-driven, multi-tissue framework for scaffold prediction, prioritization, and experimental planning. An open-source dataset comprising 2646 samples, 130 biomaterials, and 186 cell lines, including co-culture systems, across 18 tissue engineering contexts was compiled and used to benchmark ML, deep learning, tabular transformer-based, and tabular foundation models for predicting cell response and printability from pre-fabrication variables. The best-performing models achieved weighted F1-scores of 0.773 for cell response and 0.806 for printability. These predictive outputs were subsequently integrated through the Weighted Synergistic Scaffold Quality (WSSQ) metric, which combines cell response and printability using adjustable weights to provide a unified criterion for candidate ranking. WSSQ was then incorporated into a Bayesian optimization framework to search user-defined biomaterial compositions and printing-parameter ranges and prioritize candidate scaffold formulations for experimental evaluation. To make the complete workflow accessible to researchers, MLATE V3 was implemented as an open-source web platform that enables users to select predictive models, define design spaces, perform WSSQ-based optimization, and generate step-by-step fabrication protocols through an LLM-assisted procedure-generation module. Overall, MLATE V3 provides an extensible decision-support framework that connects literature-derived data, predictive modeling, multi-objective scaffold ranking, optimization, and experimental planning. The platform is intended to narrow the experimental search space and generate candidate formulations for subsequent experimental validation rather than to serve as an experimentally validated optimizer.

3D printed graphene oxide/calcium alginate/strontium-doped hydroxyapatite composite scaffolds with enhanced osteogenic and angiogenic properties for critical-size bone defect repair
papers.abstract: The repair of critical-sized bone defects is hindered by insufficient vascularization, an unfavorable osteogenic microenvironment, and the limitations of conventional materials. Systematic studies on ternary composites of graphene oxide (GO), calcium alginate (CA), and strontium-doped hydroxyapatite (Sr-HA) remain limited, particularly regarding how different strontium substitution levels influence scaffold rheology, mechanics, ion release, osteogenic activity, and vascular-associated responses. Here, GO/CA/Sr-HA scaffolds (3D GCHs) were fabricated via direct ink writing with systematically controlled strontium substitution levels. All inks exhibited excellent shear-thinning behavior. The scaffolds showed a regular porous morphology and uniform strontium incorporation within the hydroxyapatite lattice. Notably, among the tested formulations, 3D GCH10 achieved a compressive stress of 3.42 ± 0.03 MPa at 70% strain and sustained Sr2+/Ca2+ release for 28 d. In vitro, 3D GCH10 promoted bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cell proliferation, upregulated alkaline phosphatase, OPN, and RUNX2, enhanced mineralization, and showed no cytotoxicity. In a rat cranial defect model, BV/TV increased by 214.35% versus the blank group, with superior new bone formation, collagen deposition, and CD31/α-SMA-positive vascular density. These results suggest that appropriate strontium substitution combined with GO and CA contributes to improved scaffold properties and enhanced bone regeneration, highlighting the potential of 3D GCH10 for bone tissue engineering.

papers.title: Structural and functional remodeling of large-scale cardiac tubes
papers.abstract: The functionality of tissue-engineered cardiac constructs using human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) is challenged by the cells’ immature state. To promote cell and tissue maturation, co-culture approaches, mechanical, electrical and topographical stimuli have been applied. Here, large tubular constructs (6 × 1 cm) were engineered from hiPSC-CMs and human foreskin fibroblasts (hFFs) (ratio 9:1) via a rotating mold technology in four independent experiments. A maturation regimen employing progressive uniaxial stretch imposed on cardiac tubes by a custom-designed, cost-efficient, fully three-dimensional printed stretching device ensured minimal manual intervention. Stepwise stretching (21% over 20 days) improved tissue contractility, alignment of hiPSC-CMs, sarcomere organization, and increased expression of cardiac structural genes, while maintaining tissue integrity and functionality in terms of spontaneous contractility and electrical responsiveness. The effect of modulating the stromal cell fraction on morphological and functional features of cardiac tubes was investigated in a pilot experiment. To more closely mimic native cardiac tissue and promote clinical translation, the originally applied hFFs were replaced with hiPSC-derived cardiac fibroblast-like cells. Compared with planar cardiac tissues dominating the field, our results provide translational insights into tubular constructs, better reflecting aspects of the native heart. Our progress in large-scale tissue engineering and functional outcomes paves the way toward establishing clinically relevant biological cardiac assist devices.

Optogenetic-enabled biomanufacturing of long-projecting motor tracts for neural reconstruction
papers.abstract: Tissue-engineered spinal tracts (TE-STs), a subclass of micro-tissue-engineered neural networks, are designed to replace long-range axonal pathways but are limited by the slow intrinsic growth of many neuronal subtypes, particularly spinal motor neurons. Optogenetic stimulation provides cell-type–specific, precise control of activity that may accelerate neurite extension during biofabrication. Accordingly, this study evaluates whether integrating optogenetic stimulation into the biomanufacturing process enhances motor axonal outgrowth within tailored hydrogel micro-columns in vitro. Motor neuron aggregates from embryonic rat spinal cord were generated by forced aggregation and encased within agarose micro-columns (701 µm OD, ∼300 µm ID; 3–12 mm length) to create TE-STs. Neurons were transduced to express the red-shifted channelrhodopsin ChrimsonR. Stimulation parameters were first optimized in planar cultures, where a 1-hour red-light train at 10 Hz (625 nm) maximized neurite outgrowth without significant heating. TE-STs were then stimulated at 10 Hz for 1 h at 7 d in vitro (DIV) and then fixed at 21 DIV. Groups included transduced and non-transduced neurons, each with and without light stimulation. Axonal extension was quantified within the micro-column lumen, and two-way analysis of variance was used for analysis. TE-STs exhibited robust axonal growth with organized tract architecture, preserved neuronal health, and stable motor neuron phenotype. Transduced neurons with and without light stimulation extended axons faster than non-transduced controls, whereas no differences were observed between non-transduced neurons with or without light. Notably, transduced neurons exposed to a single round of optogenetic stimulation at 7 DIV reached ∼5.5 mm of growth by 21 DIV, representing a ∼2.5-fold increase over baseline controls. Brief, targeted optogenetic activation is sufficient to accelerate axonal growth of engineered spinal motor tracts during in vitro biomanufacturing. These findings establish optogenetic stimulation as a programmable biomanufacturing input that accelerates axonal assembly through activity-dependent mechanisms while remaining compatible with scalable three-dimensional tissue fabrication.

papers.title: Airflow controlled droplet bioprinting enables high-throughput generation of iPSC-derived thymic organoids with in vivo T cell functionality
papers.abstract: The thymus is a critical organ for T cell generation. It is composed of distinct layers of thymic epithelial cells (TECs) that coordinate a complex process of antigen recognition and self-tolerance checks that result in mature populations of T cells. However, it undergoes progressive and permanent involution and loss of functionality which peaks in adolescence, rendering the tissue largely non-functional. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have emerged as promising candidates to generate organoid models of the thymus because of their autologous potential and indefinite self-renewal. Previously our group has shown the capability of generating thymic epithelial progenitor cells (TEPCs) that are able to successfully program T cells in vitro and in vivo through manual encapsulation of iPSCs in sodium-alginate capsules during differentiation. To translate this capability toward clinically relevant throughput, we present a novel method of air-jetting droplet bioprinting which is capable of producing 21 500 aggregates per milliliter of bioink. We conducted a systematic analysis of critical process parameters governing iPSC aggregation, retention, and differentiation and illustrated the interplay between airflow velocity, which governs capsule size, and crosslinker chemistry governing capsule network stability. We also determined parameters that minimize printing variability and prevent decapsulation of iPSC aggregates during differentiation. Finally, we modeled the growth rate and carrying capacity of different printing configurations, and validated manufactured organoids in vivo by generating functional murine T cell populations in athymic nude mice after decapsulation and construction with a decellularized thymus scaffold.

A 3D-printed spider silk-based functional mesh for ventral hernia repair via endogenous regeneration-promoting strategies
papers.abstract: Ventral hernia, a prevalent condition especially in the elderly, is primarily treated with mesh implantation. However, high postoperative recurrence persists due to mismatched degradation rates of biological meshes and tissue remodeling. We engineered an electrospun composite mesh (CPCM) integrating chitosan, polylactic acid, and chimeric mini-spidroin recombinant collagen to address this challenge. The CPCM was fabricated by combining 3D printing with bilateral electrospinning. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy, water contact-angle measurements, degradation assays, and uniaxial tensile testing were used to characterize its physicochemical and mechanical properties. Cytocompatibility, cell adhesion, antibacterial activity, and angiogenic effects were evaluated. A rat abdominal wall defect model was used to assess biocompatibility, vascularization, collagen remodeling, and repair efficacy through histological staining, immunofluorescence, Western blotting, and quantitative reverse transcription PCR. The CPCM exhibited favorable physicochemical and mechanical properties, gradual degradation, satisfactory cytocompatibility, enhanced cell adhesion, and significant antibacterial activity. CPCM implantation was associated with a repair-associated macrophage response and increased vascular density and vascular maturation during the early repair phase. At 12 weeks, the CPCM group exhibited greater collagen deposition, a higher collagen I/III ratio, more coherently organized collagen bundles, and improved mechanical performance of the repaired abdominal wall. molecular analyses further supported the involvement of TGF-β/Smad signaling in the fibroblast response to CPCM. CPCM demonstrated favorable physicochemical properties, antibacterial activity, and biocompatibility, and supported vascularization, repair-associated macrophage responses and collagen remodeling during abdominal wall repair. These findings suggest that CPCM may provide a promising multifunctional biodegradable mesh for abdominal wall reconstruction, while the contribution of TGF-β/Smad signaling to its regenerative effects warrants further investigation.
